text.p: With a month to go before the May 13 budget, it is worth reviewing the government's current fiscal target -- full-year savings of at least A$2 billion.
The government came to office with a commitment to a balanced budget in 1997/98, and the 1996 budget was expected to achieve this with its full-year savings of A$7 billion.

Treasury's calculations proved erroneous, however, and the mid-year review issued at the end of January revealed that the government would only achieve nothing better than a A$4 billion deficit in 1997/98. Even in the following year the deficit would be A$2 billion.

So Treasurer Peter Costello shifted his ground and the fiscal target became a balanced budget in 1998/99. He specifically said at the time he would not try to find the savings necessary for a 1997/98 balance.
Assuming no further changes in fiscal projections, the government must therefore be aiming for full-year savings of at least A$2 billion to meet the 1998/99 target.
Fiscal measures typically take a year or two to ramp-up and the government would have to be extremely tough to find the A$4 billion in savings for 1997/98 alone.
So a realistic guess at the May budget might be savings worth A$1 billion or so in 1997/98 and A$2 billion or so in subsequent years.
The crucial assumption is that changing fiscal projections do not move the ground under our feet.
Much larger measures are conceivable if government finances are in worse shape than thought in January.

If the budget is in better shape than thought, the government would probably still go ahead with some cuts, to give it room for error and maybe some money to spend on giveaways before the election due in early 1999.
THE FINE ART OF WATCHING THE LEAKS
You have to take some budget leaks with a pinch of salt.
Some are just politically impossible proposals from the Finance Department.
The May 13 budget is a month away and the government is now well into the process of identifying some fiscal gains.
We can expect plenty of leaks over the next four weeks.

Treasurer Peter Costello has identified so-called tax expenditures as a key target for this year's budget -- by complaining since the 1996 budget about how much it costs for tax exemptions for this or that, and how some people get a break while others pay for it.
The reason for targetting tax expenditures is that further cuts in real spending must be getting very hard to find, shifting attention to the revenue side of the budget.
But while the implementation of further spending cuts may be increasingly difficult for the government, the advocacy of them by the Finance Department is no problem at all.

So watch out for leaks in newspapers and other media. Don't take them too seriously if they look like politically untenable, off-the-rack submissions that Finance probably trots out every year as part of its mission to restrain spending.

Naturally when Finance proposes some shocking cut to a department, the department's officers sing like canaries, often leaking the proposal to a friendly journalist who specialises in that department and who will write a suitably outraged report.
On the other hand, officials might sing just as much about real cuts, so one has to be discerning.
One very senior government minister conceded off-the-record last year that the government's politically brilliant 1996 budget strategy had been no strategy at all.
Yes, this minister said, the government had taken the sting out of budget day by announcing many of the cuts in the preceeding month.
But it had no choice, he said. The public service was leaking almost everything the government was going to do and a whole lot that it wasn't.
Simply to contain damage the government repeatedly had to formally announce the nasties to stop the speculation.
Often the announcement created only moderately bad publicity because the cuts weren't as bad as the Finance Department horrors that had already leaked.
Then when the full budget was announced, everyone was shocked to find only a moderate amount of bad news (note: news has to be new) floating around in all the fiscal responsibility.
The result: Treasurer Peter Costello cut the budget by more than former Labor treasurer John Dawkins had managed in 1993 but copped less than half the political flak.
All thanks to the leaks.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
